hints: Start by sorting the four responses into two groups - those that reduce heat loss to the environment and those that increase heat production inside the body.
Think about blood flow and sweat at the skin surface - how does moving warm blood away from the surface or keeping the skin dry change radiation and evaporation?
Think about skeletal muscle activity and the layer of air next to the skin - where does the extra heat come from and what traps warm air?

Link each response to its physics: less surface blood flow means less heat radiated, muscle contraction releases heat from respiration, trapped air insulates, less evaporation means less heat removed.
walkthrough:
Vasoconstriction Reduces Heat Loss From Skin**
When core temperature falls, the hypothalamus causes arterioles near the skin surface to constrict. Less warm blood reaches the surface, so a steeper temperature gradient is kept between core and skin and less heat is lost by radiation, conduction and convection.

Shivering Generates Extra Heat**
Shivering is rapid, involuntary contraction and relaxation of skeletal muscles. Muscle contraction requires ATP from aerobic respiration, and much of that energy is released as heat, warming the blood and core.

Raised Hairs and Less Sweat Conserve Heat**
Contraction of erector pili muscles raises hairs, trapping a thicker still layer of air next to the skin. Still air is a poor conductor, so it insulates. At the same time sweat glands secrete less sweat, so less heat is used to evaporate water from the skin surface.

Final answer: Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles reduces blood flow to the skin surface so less heat is lost by radiation and conduction; shivering by rapid muscle contraction generates heat from respiration; erection of hairs traps a layer of air which insulates and reduces heat loss; reduced sweat production decreases evaporative heat loss.

hints: Think about which part of the body loses heat to cold air and how changing shape changes the area exposed.
walkthrough:
Smaller Exposed Surface Means Less Heat Loss**
Heat is lost across the body surface. By curling into a ball the animal hides limbs and belly and exposes the minimum surface area to cold air, so the rate of heat loss by radiation and convection falls and core temperature is conserved.
Final answer: Curling up decreases the surface area exposed to the cold, so less heat is lost and core heat is conserved.

hints: Look at the shape of each line in Fig. 6.3 - which line stays almost flat and which line climbs steeply with the x-axis?
Read off values with units to prove the pattern - pick the Sitatunga core temperature range and the Nile monitor core temperature at low and high environmental temperatures.
Remember to state the contrast clearly: constant core temperature versus core temperature following the environment, supported by paired figures in $^{\circ}C$.
walkthrough:
Sitatunga Shows Endothermic Constancy**
The top line is almost horizontal. Even when environmental temperature increases from $5^{\circ}C$ to $40^{\circ}C$, Sitatunga core temperature stays within a narrow range, about $36^{\circ}C$ to $38^{\circ}C$. This is physiological thermoregulation.

Nile Monitor Follows The Environment**
The lower line rises steeply. At an environmental temperature of $5^{\circ}C$ its core is only about $5^{\circ}C$, at $20^{\circ}C$ environment its core is about $20^{\circ}C$, and at $40^{\circ}C$ environment its core is about $36^{\circ}C$. Core temperature increases as environmental temperature increases.

Use Figures To Secure Marks**
A good description always quotes data with units. Compare like with like: at $20^{\circ}C$ environment, Sitatunga is about $38^{\circ}C$ while Nile monitor is about $20^{\circ}C$. Or show change in one animal: Nile monitor rises from about $9^{\circ}C$ at $10^{\circ}C$ environment to about $31^{\circ}C$ at $30^{\circ}C$ environment.

Final answer: Sitatunga maintains an almost constant core temperature of about $36^{\circ}C$ to $38^{\circ}C$ as environmental temperature rises from $5^{\circ}C$ to $40^{\circ}C$; Nile monitor core temperature rises with environmental temperature, from about $5^{\circ}C$ at $5^{\circ}C$ environment to about $36^{\circ}C$ at $40^{\circ}C$ environment, e.g. $20^{\circ}C$ core at $20^{\circ}C$ environment and $31^{\circ}C$ core at $30^{\circ}C$ environment.

hints: Think about what a slow, cold lizard cannot do well - finding food or escaping from something else.
walkthrough:
Cold Muscles Mean Slow Responses**
At low environmental temperature the Nile monitor has a low body temperature, so enzyme and muscle activity are slow. If it is inactive it cannot move quickly to hunt prey or to avoid being eaten itself.
Final answer: Inactivity makes it less able to catch prey / feed or to escape predators.

hints: Start from the idea of an ideal value - what does the body compare its actual core temperature against?
Think about what happens after a rise or fall is detected - does the response make the change bigger or smaller?
Finish the loop: the effect of the response on the original change brings the system back toward the starting point.
walkthrough:
A Set Point Is The Reference**
Negative feedback control has a set point, the normal or ideal core temperature, about $37^{\circ}C$ in mammals. Receptors and the hypothalamus constantly monitor the actual temperature against this set point.

Deviation Triggers An Opposite Response**
If core temperature rises or falls, that fluctuation is detected. The control centre then activates effectors that work in the opposite direction to the change, for example vasodilation and sweating after a rise, or vasoconstriction and shivering after a fall.

Change Is Reversed To Restore Stability**
Because the response reverses the original change, the deviation is corrected and core temperature returns toward the set point. That is why it is called negative - the output negates the input change, keeping conditions within narrow limits.

Final answer: A constant set point / normal value is maintained; any rise or fall / deviation from the set point is detected and triggers responses that reverse / counteract the change, returning the value toward the set point.
